new_head_para: So the engagement that took place near Caphyae, then, turned out in this way. When the Megalopolitans learned that the Aetolians were encamped near Methydrium, they came at the call of the trumpet, with their whole population, to give aid on the day immediately following the battle.

new_head_para: These, then, are the true causes of the outflow of the Pontus, deriving their credibility not from merchants’ tales, but from observation according to nature—than which it is not easy to find a more accurate method. And since we have settled on this topic, we must leave nothing idle or resting on mere assertion—as most writers are accustomed to do—but must employ a more demonstrative manner of exposition, so that we leave none of the points under inquiry unresolved for our attentive readers.
note: Greek θεω-/ρίας runs on; only defect is stray space after the dash ('nature— than'); removed.

new_head_para: And as to the size of the bank just described, and in general the quantity of stones, timber, and earth carried down by the rivers, there is no reason whatever to be skeptical—for that would be foolish—when we see before our own eyes how some chance torrent in a short time will often gouge out and cut through sheer places, carry off every kind of timber, earth, and stone, and pile up such mounds that at times it alters those same places and makes them unrecognizable in a brief span of time. From all this it is not reasonable to wonder how rivers of such size and such character, flowing continuously, accomplish some of the effects described and in the end fill up the Pontus.
note: Greek ἐν βραχεῖ χρόνῳ / τοὺς αὐτοὺς τόπους runs on; old 'a place … — these same places' would repeat and leave a stray dash.
Greek φέρεται / διὰ πόρου; no gap. 'falls short of' for ἀπολιπών ('leaving behind') is loose, but outside seam scope.

new_head_para: But when, on top of all this, the Gauls under Comontorius fell upon them as well, they were brought to the very brink of ruin. These Gauls had set out from their homeland together with Brennus; but having escaped the disaster at Delphi and reached the Hellespont, they did not cross over into Asia. Instead they stayed where they were, drawn to the region around Byzantium for its appeal.
note: Greek προσεπιγενομένων … / εἰς πᾶν ἦλθον περιστάσεως runs on; the leading dash at ch 46 start would double the dash, so removed.

new_head_para: But since most of the Greeks paid no attention, the Byzantines, driven by necessity, set about levying a duty on those sailing into the Pontus. Since the Byzantines’ collection of a toll on goods exported from the Pontus proved a serious loss and inconvenience to everyone, people regarded it as an outrage, and all the seafaring traders directed their complaints against the Rhodians, on the grounds that the Rhodians were considered the leading power at sea. It was out of this that the war arose, the war I am now about to recount.
note: Greek ἐνεχείρησαν παρ- / αγωγιάζειν runs on; leading dash at ch 47 start would double the dash, so removed.

new_head_para: At once they dispatched envoys to Prusias, urging him too to join the war; for they knew that Prusias was already at odds, on several grounds, with the Byzantines. The Byzantines, for their part, did much the same thing: they sent envoys both to Attalus and to Achaeus, asking them for help.
note: Greek πρὸς τοὺς / Βυζαντίους runs on; leading dash at ch 48 start would double the dash, so removed.

new_head_para: So the Byzantines, cheated of their own hopes and hard pressed by the war on every side, began to look about for a respectable way out of their situation. And when Cavarus, the king of the Gauls, arrived at Byzantium and showed himself eager to put an end to the war, ambitiously extending his hands in mediation, both Prusias and the Byzantines agreed to his proposals.
note: Greek ἐξαγωγὴν περιέβλεπον εὐ- / σχήμονα runs on; leading dash at ch 52 start would double the dash, so removed.
